text: Lesson four made Bronze ingestion incremental, so only new source files land there each run, instead of re-reading everything every single night. But that creates a new problem one layer up, because the old Silver step just truncated and rebuilt silver.sales_clean from scratch every night, and that no longer makes sense once Bronze itself is incremental. This lesson fixes it with a real Delta Lake upsert, instead of a full rewrite.

Rebuilding all of Silver every night was fine when Bronze was small enough to fully reprocess in a reasonable amount of time. It isn't anymore, and honestly it was always a little wasteful, since most rows in Silver haven't actually changed since yesterday's run. What Silver actually needs instead is an upsert: update any transaction that's already there if it happened to arrive corrected, and insert any transaction that's brand new to the table. Delta Lake has a real statement built for exactly this situation, and it's called MERGE INTO.

Here's the exact pattern this pipeline uses. MERGE INTO silver.sales_clean as the target table, USING bronze_incremental — just today's new rows, not the entire Bronze table — as the source. The two are matched ON transaction_id. WHEN MATCHED, UPDATE SET star overwrites that existing row's columns with the freshly incoming values. WHEN NOT MATCHED, INSERT star adds it to the table as a brand-new row that Silver has never seen before.

The exact same operation also works in PySpark, through the DeltaTable API. Load silver.sales_clean as a DeltaTable object, call merge against the incremental source DataFrame using that same transaction_id condition, then chain whenMatchedUpdateAll and whenNotMatchedInsertAll before calling execute. Same logic, same match key, just a different syntax for teams that prefer PySpark over raw SQL.

That match key is really the part worth getting exactly right. store_id identifies a store, not one single sale — every transaction at that store shares the same store_id, so matching on it would wrongly treat completely unrelated sales as if they were the same row. sale_date identifies a day, not a sale either — a single busy store can easily have thousands of transactions on one day. transaction_id is the one column in this entire schema that uniquely identifies a single real sale, which is exactly what a safe MERGE match key needs to be.

Get that match key right, and this MERGE INTO statement becomes the correct reference version this course keeps coming back to — lessons thirteen through fifteen later compare a broken production merge directly against exactly this pattern to find the real bug. Next lesson, you'll see a concrete late-arriving sale, and walk through why this exact design still gets its date right without any extra code.
